<SinceRelease version="2.9.0" product="tsdb" />

The more data you have, the more likely you are to run a more sophisticated analysis on it. When a simple one-level aggregation is not enough, {C.TIMESCALE_DB} lets you create {C.CAGG}s on top of other {C.CAGG}s. This way, you summarize data at different levels of granularity, while still saving resources with precomputing.

For example, you might have an hourly {C.CAGG} that summarizes minute-by-minute
data. To get a daily summary, you can create a new {C.CAGG} on top
of your hourly aggregate. This is more efficient than creating the daily
aggregate on top of the original {C.HYPERTABLE}, because you can reuse the
calculations from the hourly aggregate.

## Create a {C.CAGG} on top of another {C.CAGG}

Creating a {C.CAGG} on top of another {C.CAGG} works the
same way as creating it on top of a {C.HYPERTABLE}. In your query, select from a
{C.CAGG} rather than from the {C.HYPERTABLE}, and use the time-bucketed
column from the existing {C.CAGG} as your time column.

For more information, see the instructions for
[creating a {C.CAGG}](/build/continuous-aggregates/create-a-continuous-aggregate).

## Use {C.RTAGG} with hierarchical {C.CAGG}s

<RealTimeAgg />

{C.RTAGG_CAP}s always return up-to-date data in response to queries. They accomplish this by
joining the materialized data in the {C.CAGG} with unmaterialized
raw data from the source table or view.

When {C.CAGG}s are stacked, each {C.CAGG} is only aware
of the layer immediately below. The joining of unmaterialized data happens
recursively until it reaches the bottom layer, giving you access to recent data
down to that layer.

If you keep all {C.CAGG}s in the stack as {C.RTAGG}s, the
bottom layer is the source {C.HYPERTABLE}. That means every {C.CAGG} in
the stack has access to all recent data.

If there is a non-real-time {C.CAGG} somewhere in the stack, the
recursive joining stops at that non-real-time {C.CAGG}. Higher-level
{C.CAGG}s don't receive any unmaterialized data from lower levels.

For example, say you have the following {C.CAGG}s:

- A real-time hourly {C.CAGG} on the source {C.HYPERTABLE}
- A real-time daily {C.CAGG} on the hourly {C.CAGG}
- A non-real-time, or materialized-only, monthly {C.CAGG} on the
  daily {C.CAGG}
- A real-time yearly {C.CAGG} on the monthly {C.CAGG}

Queries on the hourly and daily {C.CAGG}s include real-time,
non-materialized data from the source {C.HYPERTABLE}. Queries on the monthly
{C.CAGG} only return already-materialized data. Queries on the
yearly {C.CAGG} return materialized data from the yearly {C.CAGG}
itself, plus more recent data from the monthly {C.CAGG}.
However, the data is limited to what is already materialized in the monthly
{C.CAGG}, and doesn't get even more recent data from the source
{C.HYPERTABLE}. This happens because the materialized-only {C.CAGG}
provides a stopping point, and the yearly {C.CAGG} is unaware of any
layers beyond that stopping point. This is similar to
[how stacked views work in {C.PG}](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rules-views.html).

To make queries on the yearly {C.CAGG} access all recent data, you
can either:

- Make the monthly {C.CAGG} real-time, or
- Redefine the yearly {C.CAGG} on top of the daily {C.CAGG}.

![Example of hierarchical continuous aggregates in a finance application](https://assets.timescale.com/docs/images/cagg_hierarchy.webp)

## Roll up calculations

When summarizing already-summarized data, be aware of how stacked calculations
work. Not all calculations return the correct result if you stack them.

For example, if you take the maximum of several subsets, then take the maximum
of the maximums, you get the maximum of the entire set. But if you take the
average of several subsets, then take the average of the averages, that can
result in a different figure than the average of all the data.

To simplify such calculations when using {C.CAGG}s on top of
{C.CAGG}s, you can use the [{C.HYPERFUNC}](/build/data-management/understand-hyperfunctions) from
{C.TOOLKIT_LONG}, such as the [statistical aggregates](/reference/toolkit/statistical-and-regression-analysis/stats_agg-one-variable/stats_agg). These
{C.HYPERFUNC} are designed with a two-step aggregation pattern that allows you
to roll them up into larger buckets. The first step creates a summary aggregate
that can be rolled up, just as a maximum can be rolled up. You can store this
aggregate in your {C.CAGG}. Then, you can call an accessor function
as a second step when you query from your {C.CAGG}. This accessor
takes the stored data from the summary aggregate and returns the final result.

For example, you can create an hourly {C.CAGG} using `percentile_agg`
over a {C.HYPERTABLE}, like this:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW response_times_hourly
WITH (timescaledb.continuous)
AS SELECT
    time_bucket('1 h'::interval, ts) as bucket,
    api_id,
    avg(response_time_ms),
    percentile_agg(response_time_ms) as percentile_hourly
FROM response_times
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

To then stack another daily {C.CAGG} over it, you can use a `rollup`
function, like this:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW response_times_daily
WITH (timescaledb.continuous)
AS SELECT
    time_bucket('1 d'::interval, bucket) as bucket_daily,
    api_id,
    mean(rollup(percentile_hourly)) as mean,
    rollup(percentile_hourly) as percentile_daily
FROM response_times_hourly
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

The `mean` function of the {C.TOOLKIT_LONG} is used to calculate the concrete
mean value of the rolled up values. The additional `percentile_daily` attribute
contains the raw rolled up values, which can be used in an additional {C.CAGG}
on top of this {C.CAGG} (for example a {C.CAGG}
for the daily values).

For more information and examples about using `rollup` functions to stack
calculations, see the [`percentile_agg` API documentation](/reference/toolkit/percentile-approximation/uddsketch/percentile_agg).

## Restrictions

There are some restrictions when creating a {C.CAGG} on top of
another {C.CAGG}. In most cases, these restrictions are in place to
ensure valid time-bucketing:

- You can only create a {C.CAGG} on top of a finalized {C.CAGG}.
  This new finalized format is the default for all {C.CAGG}s
  created since {C.TIMESCALE_DB} 2.7. If you need to create a {C.CAGG}
  on top of a {C.CAGG} in the old format, you need to
  [migrate your {C.CAGG}](/build/continuous-aggregates/migrate) to the new format first.

- The {C.TIME_BUCKET} of a {C.CAGG} should be greater than or equal to
  the {C.TIME_BUCKET} of the underlying {C.CAGG}. It also needs to be
  a multiple of the underlying {C.TIME_BUCKET}. For example, you can rebucket an
  hourly {C.CAGG} into a new {C.CAGG} with {C.TIME_BUCKET}s
  of 6 hours. You can't rebucket the hourly {C.CAGG} into
  a new {C.CAGG} with {C.TIME_BUCKET}s of 90 minutes, because 90
  minutes is not a multiple of 1 hour.

- A {C.CAGG} with a fixed-width {C.TIME_BUCKET} can't be created on
  top of a {C.CAGG} with a variable-width {C.TIME_BUCKET}. Fixed-width
  {C.TIME_BUCKET}s are {C.TIME_BUCKET}s defined in seconds, minutes, hours, and days,
  because those time intervals are always the same length. Variable-width
  {C.TIME_BUCKET}s are {C.TIME_BUCKET}s defined in months or years, because those time
  intervals vary by the month or on leap years. This limitation prevents a
  case such as trying to rebucket monthly buckets into `61 day` buckets, where
  there is no good mapping between {C.TIME_BUCKET}s for month combinations such as
  July/August (62 days).

  Note that even though weeks are fixed-width intervals, you can't use monthly
  or yearly {C.TIME_BUCKET}s on top of weekly {C.TIME_BUCKET}s for the same reason.
  The number of weeks in a month or year is usually not an integer.

  However, you can stack a variable-width {C.TIME_BUCKET} on top of a fixed-width
  {C.TIME_BUCKET}. For example, creating a monthly {C.CAGG} on top of
  a daily {C.CAGG} works, and is one of the main use cases for
  this feature.
